```{python}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import sqlite3
from datetime import date
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

# Same module build_pages.py uses, so a link written here and the page written
# there can never disagree about a URL.
from slugs import all_slugs

DB = Path(__file__).parent / "denovo.db" if "__file__" in dir() else Path("denovo.db")
conn = sqlite3.connect(DB)

# Site build date, surfaced in the footer's 'Last updated' line. Reflects when
# Quarto rendered the site (i.e., when a push or scheduled workflow last
# rebuilt gh-pages), which is a close proxy for when the catalog was refreshed.
build_date = date.today().strftime("%-d %B %Y")

pubs = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT p.id, p.title, p.publication_date AS date, p.publication_type AS type,
           p.publisher, p.journal, p.doi, p.url, p.version,
           -- author_display, not author: two different researchers share the
           -- name 'Xiang Zhang', and every chart aggregates on this string.
           --
           -- ORDER BY goes INSIDE the aggregate (SQLite 3.44+; the runner has
           -- 3.53). A trailing `ORDER BY pa.author_order` after the WHERE --
           -- which is what this was -- orders the subquery's RESULT ROWS, of
           -- which there is exactly one, and leaves the concatenation in scan
           -- order. That came out as author.id order, so the byline of
           -- publication 74 read "Kevin Eloff, Konstantinos Kalogeropoulos,
           -- Amandla Mabona, ..." when its first author is Mabona and Eloff is
           -- fifth: Eloff is author id 1, so he led every paper he appears on.
           -- This column is not cosmetic. It is the Authors column of Browse
           -- all papers AND the BibTeX export's `author` field, whose citation
           -- key is built from the FIRST name in it, so every exported entry
           -- was keyed on the wrong person.
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(a.display_name, ', ' ORDER BY pa.author_order)
              FROM publication_author pa JOIN author_display a ON a.id = pa.author_id
              WHERE pa.publication_id = p.id) AS authors,
           -- Ordered, because the citation-flow chart labels each node with
           -- the FIRST name in this list. Unordered it was whatever the scan
           -- reached first, i.e. algorithm.id, so inserting an unrelated
           -- method could silently relabel a node. Described methods lead: a
           -- venomics paper should be labelled by the workflow it contributes,
           -- not by the sequencer it ran.
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(alg.name, ', '
                     ORDER BY pal.role = 'describes' DESC, alg.name)
              FROM publication_algorithm pal JOIN algorithm alg ON alg.id = pal.algorithm_id
              WHERE pal.publication_id = p.id) AS models,
           -- The methods this paper DESCRIBES, as opposed to every method it
           -- names. `models` above stays the full list, because the table and
           -- the BibTeX are about what a paper involved; the author-to-model
           -- graph needs the narrower one, or every venomics author becomes a
           -- PEAKS author. 53 of 494 publication_algorithm links are 'uses',
           -- and 18 of PEAKS's own 21 papers are applications of it.
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(alg.name, ', ' ORDER BY alg.name)
              FROM publication_algorithm pal JOIN algorithm alg ON alg.id = pal.algorithm_id
              WHERE pal.publication_id = p.id AND pal.role = 'describes')
             AS models_described,
           -- Repository URLs come from algorithm_repository (1-N rows per algo).
           -- Concatenate with whitespace so the OJS multi-link renderer keeps working.
           -- sort_order says which of a method's repositories is canonical,
           -- and the DESCRIBED method's repository leads, the same tie-break
           -- `models` above uses. Publication 267 links InstaNexus (which it
           -- describes) and InstaNovo (which it runs), both at sort_order 0.
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(ar.url, ' '
                     ORDER BY pal.role = 'describes' DESC, ar.sort_order, ar.url)
              FROM publication_algorithm pal
              JOIN algorithm_repository ar ON ar.algorithm_id = pal.algorithm_id
              WHERE pal.publication_id = p.id) AS repo,
           -- Resolve the paper's dominant kind / DL flag / acquisition mode from its
           -- linked algorithms. Papers linked to MULTIPLE kinds (e.g. a wildlife-
           -- proteomics workflow AND InstaNovo+) previously got 'algorithm' by
           -- LIMIT 1 lottery; the priority ORDER BY below routes each paper to
           -- the kind that reflects what IT contributes:
           --   1. downstream-application (paper IS an application) beats
           --   2. review, 3. benchmark, 4. meta (paper IS a review/benchmark/meta)
           --   5. post-processor (paper introduces a post-processor)
           --   6. adjacent (paper introduces adjacent tooling)
           --   7. algorithm (default — paper introduces a de novo algorithm)
           --
           -- Restricted to the links the paper DESCRIBES, which is what "what
           -- IT contributes" means. Measured: identical for all 357 rows to
           -- what the priority order alone returned, because a paper that uses
           -- a method almost always describes something further down the list.
           -- The filter is still worth having, since it states the rule the
           -- priority order was approximating.
           (SELECT alg.kind
              FROM publication_algorithm pal JOIN algorithm alg ON alg.id = pal.algorithm_id
              WHERE pal.publication_id = p.id AND pal.role = 'describes'
              ORDER BY CASE alg.kind
                WHEN 'downstream-application' THEN 1
                WHEN 'review'                 THEN 2
                WHEN 'benchmark'              THEN 3
                WHEN 'meta'                   THEN 4
                WHEN 'post-processor'         THEN 5
                WHEN 'adjacent'               THEN 6
                WHEN 'algorithm'              THEN 7
                ELSE 8
              END
              LIMIT 1) AS kind,
           -- For is_dl / acquisition, prefer rows where the flag is actually SET —
           -- workflow rows carry NULL, algorithm rows carry the real value.
           (SELECT alg.is_deep_learning
              FROM publication_algorithm pal JOIN algorithm alg ON alg.id = pal.algorithm_id
              WHERE pal.publication_id = p.id AND alg.is_deep_learning IS NOT NULL
              LIMIT 1) AS is_dl,
           (SELECT alg.acquisition_mode
              FROM publication_algorithm pal JOIN algorithm alg ON alg.id = pal.algorithm_id
              WHERE pal.publication_id = p.id AND alg.acquisition_mode IS NOT NULL
              LIMIT 1) AS acquisition
    FROM publication p
    ORDER BY p.publication_date
    """,
    conn,
)
pubs["year"] = pd.to_datetime(pubs["date"], errors="coerce").dt.year

top_authors = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT a.display_name AS name, COUNT(pa.publication_id) AS publications
    FROM author_display a JOIN publication_author pa ON a.id = pa.author_id
    GROUP BY a.id
    ORDER BY publications DESC
    LIMIT 20
    """,
    conn,
)

geo = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT c.name AS country,
           COUNT(DISTINCT af.id) AS affiliations,
           COUNT(DISTINCT aa.author_id) AS authors
    FROM country c
    JOIN affiliation af ON af.country_id = c.id
    LEFT JOIN author_affiliation aa ON aa.affiliation_id = af.id
    GROUP BY c.id
    ORDER BY authors DESC
    """,
    conn,
)

institutions = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT af.name AS institution, c.name AS country,
           COUNT(DISTINCT aa.author_id) AS authors
    FROM affiliation af
    JOIN country c ON af.country_id = c.id
    JOIN author_affiliation aa ON aa.affiliation_id = af.id
    GROUP BY af.name
    ORDER BY authors DESC
    LIMIT 15
    """,
    conn,
)

pub_authorship = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT pa.publication_id AS pub_id,
           a.id              AS author_id,
           a.display_name    AS author,
           af.id             AS affiliation_id,
           af.name           AS affiliation,
           ci.id             AS city_id,
           ci.name           AS city,
           ci.lat            AS lat,
           ci.lng            AS lng,
           c.name            AS country
    FROM publication_author pa
    JOIN author_display a      ON a.id = pa.author_id
    LEFT JOIN author_affiliation aa ON aa.author_id = a.id
    LEFT JOIN affiliation af   ON af.id = aa.affiliation_id
    LEFT JOIN city ci          ON ci.id = af.city_id
    LEFT JOIN country c        ON c.id = af.country_id
    """,
    conn,
)

# Co-authorship pairs, bucketed by the TOTAL author count of the paper that
# produced them. Emitting per-bucket counts (rather than one pre-summed weight)
# lets the OJS side compute Newman fractional collaboration strength
# — each pair on an n-author paper earns 1/(n-1) — and lets the reader filter
# on max-authors-per-paper reactively. Without fractional weighting a single
# 53-author consortium paper contributes a 33-node clique that swamps the graph.
coauth_edges = pd.read_sql(
    """
    WITH prolific AS (
        SELECT author_id FROM publication_author
        GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
    ),
    paper_authors AS (
        SELECT publication_id, COUNT(*) AS n_authors
        FROM publication_author GROUP BY publication_id
    )
    SELECT a1.display_name AS source, a2.display_name AS target,
           pa_count.n_authors AS n_authors,
           COUNT(*) AS papers
    FROM publication_author pa1
    JOIN publication_author pa2
      ON pa1.publication_id = pa2.publication_id
     AND pa1.author_id < pa2.author_id
    JOIN author_display a1 ON a1.id = pa1.author_id
    JOIN author_display a2 ON a2.id = pa2.author_id
    JOIN paper_authors pa_count ON pa_count.publication_id = pa1.publication_id
    WHERE pa1.author_id IN (SELECT author_id FROM prolific)
      AND pa2.author_id IN (SELECT author_id FROM prolific)
      AND pa_count.n_authors > 1
    GROUP BY a1.name, a2.name, pa_count.n_authors
    """,
    conn,
)

author_affs = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT a.display_name AS author, aff.name AS affiliation
    FROM author_display a
    JOIN author_affiliation aa ON a.id = aa.author_id
    JOIN affiliation aff ON aa.affiliation_id = aff.id
    WHERE a.id IN (
        SELECT author_id FROM publication_author
        GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
    )
    """,
    conn,
)

algorithms = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT alg.name AS model,
           alg.aliases AS aliases,
           alg.algorithm_family AS family,
           alg.short_description AS description,
           -- All repository URLs for this algorithm, ordered, space-separated.
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(url, ' ' ORDER BY sort_order, url)
              FROM algorithm_repository WHERE algorithm_id = alg.id) AS repo,
           alg.kind AS kind,
           alg.is_deep_learning AS is_dl,
           alg.acquisition_mode AS acquisition,
           alg.subdomain AS subdomain,
           -- A method's first publication is the paper that DESCRIBES it, not
           -- the first paper to mention it. Two rows differ: PepSeq and manual
           -- interpretation were both dated 2000-10-01 by publication 289, an
           -- application that used them, rather than by the Micromass manual
           -- (2001-12-10) and the Current Protocols tutorial (2002-03-01) that
           -- actually document them. COALESCE is a safety net: every algorithm
           -- with a link has a 'describes' link today, and that is an invariant
           -- worth re-checking after any role edit, but an empty axis value
           -- would drop a method off the swim lane silently.
           COALESCE(
             MIN(CASE WHEN pal.role = 'describes' THEN p.publication_date END),
             MIN(p.publication_date)) AS first_pub
    FROM algorithm alg
    LEFT JOIN publication_algorithm pal ON alg.id = pal.algorithm_id
    LEFT JOIN publication p ON pal.publication_id = p.id
    GROUP BY alg.id
    ORDER BY first_pub
    """,
    conn,
)

venues = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT journal AS venue, publication_type AS type, COUNT(*) AS papers
    FROM publication
    WHERE journal IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY journal, publication_type
    ORDER BY papers DESC
    """,
    conn,
)

# All authors with their affiliations and countries. Fuels the Browse-authors table.
author_details = pd.read_sql(
    """
    -- a.email is deliberately NOT selected. Nothing on the page consumes it,
    -- but ojs_define inlines every column into index.html, so selecting it
    -- published all 78 stored addresses in the page source for scrapers to
    -- harvest, for zero benefit. They stay in the DB for provenance.
    SELECT a.id AS id, a.display_name AS name,
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT af.name || COALESCE(' / ' || af.department, '')
                     ORDER BY af.name || COALESCE(' / ' || af.department, ''))
              FROM author_affiliation aa JOIN affiliation af ON af.id = aa.affiliation_id
              WHERE aa.author_id = a.id) AS affiliations,
           (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT c.name ORDER BY c.name)
              FROM author_affiliation aa
              JOIN affiliation af ON af.id = aa.affiliation_id
              JOIN country c ON c.id = af.country_id
              WHERE aa.author_id = a.id) AS countries
    FROM author_display a
    ORDER BY a.name
    """,
    conn,
)

# Citation edges from Crossref + Semantic Scholar (built offline via
# build_citations.py). Each edge tagged with its provenance.
citations = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT pc.citing_id, pc.cited_id, pc.source
    FROM publication_citation pc
    JOIN publication citing ON citing.id = pc.citing_id
    JOIN publication cited ON cited.id = pc.cited_id
    WHERE date(citing.publication_date) >= date(cited.publication_date)
    """,
    conn,
)

# Explicit preprint -> peer-reviewed links (built offline via build_versions.py
# from bioRxiv's `published` field, Crossref is-preprint-of relations, exact
# normalised-title matches, and human-reviewed fuzzy candidates). Before this
# table existed the lifecycle chart GUESSED the relation by bucketing on
# (first algorithm name, version) and greedily pairing on date, which misread
# papers with several algorithm links and could never pair a paper with none.
pub_versions = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT preprint_id, published_id, source
    FROM publication_version
    ORDER BY preprint_id
    """,
    conn,
)

# OpenAlex 2-year mean citedness per peer-reviewed venue (built offline via
# build_journal_metrics.py). Methodologically equivalent to the JCR Impact
# Factor formula but computed over the open Crossref-aggregated citation graph.
journal_impact = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT journal, two_yr_citedness, h_index, year_collected
    FROM journal_impact
    """,
    conn,
)

# Global citation counts per publication from OpenAlex (built offline via
# build_publication_impact.py). `cited_by_count` is OpenAlex's global count for
# the matched work, not just citations from papers in this catalog.
publication_impact = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT publication_id, openalex_id, cited_by_count, match_method,
           match_score, year_collected, fetched_at
    FROM publication_impact
    """,
    conn,
)

# Code-activity metrics per repository (built offline via build_repo_metrics.py
# using the gh CLI). Joined back to algorithms so the UI can group by method.
# Each algorithm may have multiple repos; we pick the primary (lowest sort_order).
repo_metrics = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT alg.name        AS model,
           alg.algorithm_family AS family,
           ar.url          AS url,
           rm.stars,
           rm.forks,
           rm.open_issues,
           rm.closed_issues,
           rm.open_prs,
           rm.closed_prs,
           rm.last_pushed,
           rm.latest_release,
           rm.fetched_at
    FROM algorithm_repository ar
    JOIN algorithm alg            ON alg.id = ar.algorithm_id
    JOIN repository_metrics rm    ON rm.url = ar.url
    ORDER BY rm.stars DESC NULLS LAST
    """,
    conn,
)

# FIRST APPEARANCE OF EACH METHODOLOGICAL FAMILY.
# The only dataset that covers the field's whole 42-year span. The wave chart
# squashes the sparse early years against a linear count axis, and the
# architectures swim lane now gives all 52 families a lane, but it is 6069 px of
# scroll and spends 20 of its 91 height units on Transformer (AR) alone, so the
# classical era is still a thin band at the top of a very tall chart. Ten of the
# families outside the 13 hand-tuned bands first appeared before 2005.
# One row per family, dated by the earliest publication of its earliest method.
family_firsts = pd.read_sql(
    """
    WITH per_method AS (
        SELECT alg.id                  AS alg_id,
               alg.algorithm_family    AS family,
               alg.name                AS method,
               alg.kind                AS kind,
               alg.is_deep_learning    AS is_dl,
               MIN(p.publication_date) AS first_date,
               MIN(p.id)               AS pub_id
        FROM algorithm alg
        JOIN publication_algorithm pa ON pa.algorithm_id = alg.id
        JOIN publication p            ON p.id = pa.publication_id
        -- Describing papers only, for the same reason as first_pub above: this
        -- chart dates a family by when its earliest method APPEARED.
        WHERE COALESCE(alg.algorithm_family, '') <> ''
          AND pa.role = 'describes'
        GROUP BY alg.id
    ),
    ranked AS (
        SELECT per_method.*,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY family
                                  ORDER BY first_date, alg_id) AS rn,
               COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY family)          AS n_methods
        FROM per_method
    )
    SELECT r.family,
           r.first_date,
           r.method  AS first_method,
           r.kind    AS first_kind,
           r.is_dl   AS first_is_dl,
           r.n_methods,
           r.pub_id  AS first_pub_id,
           p.title   AS first_title,
           p.journal AS first_journal,
           p.doi     AS first_doi,
           p.url     AS first_url
    FROM ranked r
    JOIN publication p ON p.id = r.pub_id
    WHERE r.rn = 1
    ORDER BY r.first_date
    """,
    conn,
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Public benchmarks. Written by build_benchmarks.py from
# bittremieuxlab/denovo_benchmarks; see the docstring there for what the numbers
# are. Everything the charts need is three small frames plus a provenance dict.
#
# is_latest = 1 keeps one row per (tool, dataset): the newest version of that
# tool which ran on it. The rule needs a natural version comparison with an
# `_old` suffix exception, so the builder applies it and flags the row.
benchmark_results = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT r.dataset,
           d.category,
           d.cat_group,
           r.tool,
           t.display_name,
           t.version,
           t.n_datasets,
           t.algorithm_id,
           alg.algorithm_family AS family,
           r.ap_peptide,
           r.ap_aa
    FROM benchmark_result r
    JOIN benchmark_dataset d ON d.name = r.dataset
    JOIN benchmark_tool t    ON t.tool = r.tool
    LEFT JOIN algorithm alg  ON alg.id = t.algorithm_id
    WHERE r.is_latest = 1
    ORDER BY r.tool, r.dataset
    """,
    conn,
)

benchmark_curves = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT c.tool, t.display_name, alg.algorithm_family AS family,
           t.n_datasets, c.level, c.coverage, c.precision
    FROM benchmark_curve c
    JOIN benchmark_tool t   ON t.tool = c.tool
    LEFT JOIN algorithm alg ON alg.id = t.algorithm_id
    ORDER BY c.level, c.tool, c.coverage
    """,
    conn,
)

# Dataset order inside each category group, so the heatmap's columns are stable
# between renders rather than following whatever order the join returns.
benchmark_datasets = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT name, category, cat_group, n_tools FROM benchmark_dataset "
    "ORDER BY cat_group, category, name", conn)

benchmark_source = dict(conn.execute("SELECT key, value FROM benchmark_source"))

# The application areas. The label and the one-line blurb are data, shared with
# build_pages.py, which generates a page per area; the lane order and the
# colours stay in the OJS cells below, because those are presentation.
subdomains = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT id, name, label, blurb FROM subdomain ORDER BY id", conn)

# Datasets, for the version-ambiguity chart and the nine-species provenance
# flow. Three queries rather than one join, because the grains differ: one row
# per (paper, dataset, version) link, one per version, one per address. Joining
# them would multiply the link rows by the address count and inflate every
# paper count on the chart.
#
# dataset_usage keeps the version NULL where the paper did not determine one.
# That NULL is the whole point of the first chart, so it must survive into OJS
# rather than being coalesced to a label here: a Python-side fillna would make
# "not stated" indistinguishable from a version actually called that.
dataset_usage = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT pd.publication_id   AS pub_id,
           d.name              AS dataset,
           d.kind              AS kind,
           dv.version          AS version,
           pd.role             AS role
      FROM publication_dataset pd
      JOIN dataset d            ON d.id  = pd.dataset_id
      LEFT JOIN dataset_version dv ON dv.id = pd.dataset_version_id
     ORDER BY d.name, dv.version
""", conn)

dataset_versions = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT d.name AS dataset, d.kind, dv.id AS version_id, dv.version,
           dv.n_spectra, dv.n_train, dv.n_validation, dv.n_test,
           dv.released, dv.introduced_by
      FROM dataset d JOIN dataset_version dv ON dv.dataset_id = d.id
     ORDER BY d.name, dv.id
""", conn)

dataset_addresses = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT dv.id AS version_id, d.name AS dataset, dv.version,
           a.repository, a.accession, a.url, a.part, a.is_provenance
      FROM dataset_address a
      JOIN dataset_version dv ON dv.id = a.dataset_version_id
      JOIN dataset d          ON d.id  = dv.dataset_id
     ORDER BY a.is_provenance, d.name, dv.id, a.repository, a.accession
""", conn)

# ProteoBench: the other public benchmark, one dataset and one row per submitted
# run, written by build_proteobench.py. Its four metrics are not
# interchangeable, so all four come through and the chart lets the reader pick;
# see that script's docstring for what each one means.
proteobench = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT s.id, s.display_name, s.software, s.version, s.decoding,
           s.checkpoint, s.pb_version, s.submitted, s.n_spectra,
           s.algorithm_id, alg.algorithm_family AS family,
           m.level, m.match_type, m.precision, m.recall, m.coverage, m.auc
    FROM proteobench_submission s
    JOIN proteobench_metric m ON m.submission_id = s.id
    LEFT JOIN algorithm alg   ON alg.id = s.algorithm_id
    ORDER BY s.display_name, m.level, m.match_type
    """,
    conn,
)

proteobench_curves = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT c.submission_id, s.display_name, alg.algorithm_family AS family,
           c.level, c.match_type, c.coverage, c.precision
    FROM proteobench_curve c
    JOIN proteobench_submission s ON s.id = c.submission_id
    LEFT JOIN algorithm alg       ON alg.id = s.algorithm_id
    ORDER BY c.level, c.match_type, s.display_name, c.i
    """,
    conn,
)

proteobench_source = dict(conn.execute("SELECT key, value FROM proteobench_source"))

# One lookup replaces threading ids through seven datasets. `key` is exactly the
# string the charts ALREADY aggregate on -- a display name, an algorithm name,
# an institution name, a journal -- with publications keyed by id. That matters
# because several charts (top authors, top institutions) recompute their rows
# client-side from pubs_filtered by NAME, so no server-side id could reach them.
_slug_tables = all_slugs(conn)
_slug_tables.pop("__fallbacks__", None)

_key_sql = {
    "publications": "SELECT id, CAST(id AS TEXT) FROM publication",
    # Keyed by the subdomain NAME, which is what the charts carry.
    "subdomains":   "SELECT id, name FROM subdomain",
    "authors":      "SELECT id, display_name FROM author_display",
    "algorithms":   "SELECT id, name FROM algorithm",
    "institutions": "SELECT MIN(id), name FROM affiliation GROUP BY name",
    # Keyed by the family NAME, which is what every family-coloured chart
    # carries. Only the families with two or more methods have a page, so this
    # repeats slugs.py's HAVING clause; a family missing here is a family whose
    # lane label falls back to its single method's page.
    "families":     "SELECT MIN(id), algorithm_family FROM algorithm "
                    "WHERE COALESCE(algorithm_family, '') <> '' "
                    "GROUP BY algorithm_family HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2",
    "venues":       "SELECT MIN(id), journal FROM publication "
                    "WHERE journal IS NOT NULL AND journal <> '' GROUP BY journal",
}
_rows = []
for _kind, _sql in _key_sql.items():
    _slugs = _slug_tables[_kind]
    for _id, _key in conn.execute(_sql + " ORDER BY 1"):
        _slug = _slugs.get(int(_id))
        if _slug:
            _rows.append({"type": _kind, "key": _key, "slug": _slug})
entity_slugs = pd.DataFrame(_rows, columns=["type", "key", "slug"])

conn.close()

ojs_define(
    pubs=pubs,
    top_authors=top_authors,
    geo=geo,
    institutions=institutions,
    pub_authorship=pub_authorship,
    coauth_edges=coauth_edges,
    author_affs=author_affs,
    algorithms=algorithms,
    venues=venues,
    author_details=author_details,
    citations=citations,
    pub_versions=pub_versions,
    family_firsts=family_firsts,
    entity_slugs=entity_slugs,

    publication_impact=publication_impact,
    repo_metrics=repo_metrics,

    benchmark_curves=benchmark_curves,

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# NETWORK STATISTICS OF THE AUTHOR-MODEL BIPARTITE GRAPH
# Measured 2026-09-14. Recorded deliberately and NOT published yet.
#
# SNAPSHOT INVALIDATED 2026-09-21: repairing seven truncated bylines added 34
# authors and 61 author-paper links, several of them on multi-author papers,
# so the node and edge counts below and every figure derived from them are now
# stale. Re-measure before publishing any of them. The judgements about WHICH
# statistics are worth publishing still stand; only the numbers moved.
#
# The graph is the one built by the `author_algo_network` OJS cell further down
# ("Models and the authors behind them"): authors with >= 3 publications linked
# to version-suffixed algorithm labels. 297 nodes (150 authors, 147 models),
# 653 edges, confirmed bipartite, 8 components, giant component 247 nodes (83%).
#
# These notes live in the PYTHON chunk on purpose. Quarto embeds OJS cell source
# into _site/index.html and search.json even under `echo: false`, because the
# client-side OJS runtime needs it, so a comment next to the chart would ship to
# the live site and be full-text searchable. Python chunk comments are genuinely
# dropped from the output (verified both ways). Keep it here until published on
# purpose.
#
# Numbers are a snapshot and will drift as the catalog grows. They came from an
# ad-hoc networkx script, not a committed builder, so there is no build_*.py to
# go looking for.
#
# A statistic was judged publishable only if it is STABLE (survives changing the
# >= 3 filter or deleting a single node), INTERPRETABLE without graph theory,
# and NOT AN ARTIFACT of how the catalog was assembled. Most graph metrics fail
# at least one.
#
# WORTH PUBLISHING
#
#   1. Two papers carry the connectivity. Dropping "Living proteomics benchmark"
#      and "AI proteomics perspective" collapses the giant component from 247
#      nodes to 69, so roughly 72% of the apparent connectivity rests on two
#      multi-author consortium papers rather than on method-level collaboration.
#      The most useful number here, because it changes how the chart should be
#      read: it belongs as a caveat ON that visualisation, not as a trophy.
#      "Living proteomics benchmark" alone carries 38 co-authors, is the unique
#      node whose eccentricity equals the radius, and has betweenness 0.648.
#
#   2. Seven satellite components with no path to the giant one. Doubles as a
#      curation worklist: some are genuinely separate communities (Xuan Guo's
#      DIA cluster, the Malmstrom epitope group, the Merkley/Jenson forensics
#      pair), others are probably a co-authorship link not yet catalogued.
#
#   3. Paradigm migration. Of 593 authors with a family-tagged method, 146 touch
#      >= 2 families and 133 of those end in a different family than they
#      started. Ming Li and Bin Ma both run "Graph / DP" (2003) to
#      "Transformer (AR)" (2026 and 2023 respectively). The deep-learning
#      transition was carried by incumbents adapting, not newcomers displacing
#      them.
#
# BORDERLINE: 26 articulation points (top authors Jurgen Cox, Bin Ma, Jeroen Van
# Goey, Lennart Martens, William Stafford Noble) and 35 bridges are meaningful
# but fail the stability test, since the set depends on the arbitrary >= 3
# threshold and is partly manufactured by the same two mega-papers.
# Architectural breadth per author (Bin Ma and Pavel A. Pevzner at 5 families
# each) is really a per-author slice of finding 3.
#
# REJECTED, WITH REASONS, SO THEY ARE NOT RE-PROPOSED
#
#   * Longest simple path. NP-hard here: the giant component has 342 independent
#     cycles and not one of the 8 components is a tree (checked, because a
#     forest would have made it exactly solvable in linear time). A randomised
#     DFS exhibited a 94-node simple path, but that is an uncertifiable lower
#     bound, not an optimum.
#   * Diameter (12 hops), radius (6), mean shortest path (4.96 hops). These look
#     like the respectable choice and are not. Hops alternate author/model, so
#     12 hops is 6 collaborative steps, which no reader will infer, and the
#     value is unstable: deleting one node moved it 12 -> 14. The diameter PATH
#     is a decent narrative object and runs "CID/HCD spectra pairs" -> Yan Yan
#     -> "Spectral-library-assisted de novo" -> Kaizhong Zhang -> "PEAKS" ->
#     Ming Li -> "Living proteomics benchmark" -> Konstantinos Kalogeropoulos ->
#     "InstaNovo-P" -> Lennart Martens -> "DeNovoGUI" -> Marc Vaudel ->
#     "SearchGUI". The number itself is not worth quoting.
#   * Degree assortativity (-0.037). A null result; publishing it is noise.
#   * Betweenness ranking. Redundant with the articulation points and less
#     interpretable than "removing this person splits the network".
#   * Method concentration. Top 5 authors appear on 20% of the 128
#     algorithm/post-processor rows, top 50 on 45%. Unremarkable, no story.
#   * Newcomer share by year. Looked like the most promising finding (88% of
#     2022's new methods came from first-time teams, falling to 27% in 2025 and
#     9% in 2026) and was discarded on inspection: the "already seen" author set
#     grows monotonically, so the share declines mechanically whether or not
#     anything real changed, and 2026 was only ~70% elapsed when measured.
#     Salvageable by switching to a bounded window ("no method in the prior
#     three years") instead of a cumulative set. Do that before believing it.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Shared Plot-tip styling used across every Plot chart on the page. Matches
// the .map-tooltip CSS palette (12-13 px, roomier padding, white background
// with soft border) so the built-in Plot tip looks the same as our custom
// world-map / co-auth / bipartite HTML tooltips.
plot_tip_style = ({
  fontSize: 13,
  lineHeight: 1.35,
  textPadding: 10,
  // Plot truncates each tip line at lineWidth (20em by default, roughly 40
  // characters) and the ellipsis eats the END of the line, which is the value.
  // Several x labels here are already 29-37 characters, so the default left no
  // room for the number. None of these tips carry free text like a paper title,
  // so a wider limit costs nothing.
  lineWidth: 34,
  fill: "white",
  stroke: "#d0d7de"
})

pubs_t = transpose(pubs).map(r => ({ ...r, year: +r.year, date: r.date ? new Date(r.date) : null }))

// Shared country colour scale. Both the Top-institutions bars and the
// most-published-authors bars use this, so a country keeps the same colour in
// both. It has to be an explicit scale over the FULL country list: Plot's
// default ordinal colours are assigned per-chart from whatever domain that
// chart happens to contain, so two charts with different country sets would
// otherwise paint the same country differently.
country_color = {
  const all = Array.from(
    new Set(transpose(pub_authorship).map(r => r.country).filter(Boolean))
  ).sort()
  const palette = d3.schemeTableau10
    .concat(d3.schemeSet3, d3.schemeSet2, d3.schemePaired)
  return d3.scaleOrdinal()
    .domain(all)
    .range(all.map((_, i) => palette[i % palette.length]))
    .unknown("#c9d1d9")
}

// Shared algorithm-family colour scale, for the same reason country_color
// exists: Plot's default ordinal colours are positional, so a family's colour
// silently changes whenever the set of families present changes. That bit us
// once already: adding one 'Tooling' category to the code-activity scatter
// reshuffled every colour and turned Transformer (AR) brown. An explicit scale
// over the full family list keeps a family the same colour wherever it appears.
// The first 13 hexes are the architectures swim-lane's canonical band colours,
// so the scatter and the swim-lane now agree.
family_color_scale = {
  // Heuristic, Graph / DP and Learning-to-rank used to be pinned to three near
  // identical greys (#8a96a0, #6c757d, #5f6b7a). They are not here any more, so
  // they get a generated colour like any other family. Heuristic and Graph / DP
  // are the two oldest and therefore the two biggest lanes at the TOP of the
  // swim lane, 12.8 deltaE apart: the chart opened on two grey slabs, which is
  // the main reason it read as colourless.
  const canonical = {
    "HMM":               "#4d6a8c",
    "Decision tree":     "#7b6f43",
    "Random Forest":     "#a5673f",
    "CNN + RNN":         "#4C72B0",
    "Transformer (AR)":  "#DD8452",
    "GNN":               "#937860",
    "CNN":               "#8172B3",
    "Transformer (NAR)": "#55A868",
    "Diffusion":         "#C44E52"
  }
  // Flow is not pinned either. Its notebook colour, #937DC2, sat 5.8 deltaE
  // from CNN's #8172B3, which was the worst pair on the whole page and a real
  // ambiguity in a 71-entry legend.
  // The other 36 families get a GENERATED colour rather than a slot in a d3
  // scheme. No scheme is long enough: cycling `i % palette.length` repeats a
  // colour, which is exactly the ambiguity this scale exists to prevent, and the
  // schemes carry near-white pastels (#ffffb3, #ffed6f) that vanish as a small
  // dot. Colours are drawn instead from a 24-hue grid at FIXED CIE lightness and
  // chroma, `d3.lch(46, 58, h)`, which keeps every one equally dark: these have
  // to carry a 10 px bold label as well as a dot. LCh and not HSL because HSL at
  // one lightness renders yellow far paler than blue.
  //
  // Assignment walks families in order of FIRST APPEARANCE and picks, for each,
  // the grid hue furthest in CIE Lab from its neighbours in that order. Both
  // swim lanes and "The long view" lay families out chronologically, so a
  // family's neighbours in this walk are the lanes it will actually sit next
  // to, which is the only adjacency the eye compares. Alphabetical assignment
  // measured four adjacent pairs under the deltaE >= 20 bar, worst 11.1; this
  // measured none. The order is a property of the data, not of one chart, so
  // the scale stays chart-independent.
  const lab = hex => {
    const [r, g, b] = [1, 3, 5].map(i => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255)
      .map(c => c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4)
    const X = (0.4124 * r + 0.3576 * g + 0.1805 * b) / 0.95047
    const Y =  0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b
    const Z = (0.0193 * r + 0.1192 * g + 0.9505 * b) / 1.08883
    const f = t => t > 0.008856 ? Math.cbrt(t) : 7.787 * t + 16 / 116
    return [116 * f(Y) - 16, 500 * (f(X) - f(Y)), 200 * (f(Y) - f(Z))]
  }
  const dE = (p, q) => {
    const a = lab(p), b = lab(q)
    return Math.hypot(a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1], a[2] - b[2])
  }
  const first_pub = d3.rollup(
    transpose(algorithms).filter(r => r.family && r.first_pub),
    v => d3.min(v, r => r.first_pub),
    r => r.family
  )
  // The author-model graph labels a FAMILY-LESS algorithm by its kind, so
  // 'Reviews', 'Adjacent tools (misc)' and 'Application: venomics' are families
  // as far as a legend is concerned. They have to be coloured here or they all
  // fall through to the single unknown fallback: consolidating that chart's own
  // palette into this scale is what exposed it, with 20-odd legend entries
  // coming out the same brown. Built from the same columns the graph reads, so
  // the two cannot drift; they sort last because they have no first-appearance
  // date of their own.
  const pseudo = ["Reviews", "Benchmarks", "Meta / catalogs",
                  "Post-processors (misc)", "Adjacent tools (misc)"]
    .concat(Array.from(new Set(
      transpose(algorithms)
        .filter(r => r.kind === "downstream-application")
        .map(r => `Application: ${r.subdomain ?? "misc"}`))).sort())
  const ordered = Array.from(new Set(
    transpose(algorithms).map(r => r.family).filter(Boolean)
  )).sort((a, b) =>
    d3.ascending(first_pub.get(a) ?? "9999", first_pub.get(b) ?? "9999") ||
    d3.ascending(a, b)).concat(pseudo)
  // The candidate palette is 24 hues at two lightnesses and two chromas, 96
  // colours, not 24 hues at one of each. With 71 families to colour (49 real
  // plus the graph's 22 pseudo-families) a single-hue-ring palette runs out
  // after 24 and the picker below starts reusing: the legend came out as
  // alternating greens and purples. Lightness 40 and 54 both carry a bold
  // label on white, which is the constraint that keeps this grid small.
  const grid = d3.cross(d3.range(24), [40, 54], [42, 62])
    .map(([h, l, c]) => d3.lch(l, c, h * 15).formatHex())
  const map = new Map(Object.entries(canonical))
  const taken = Object.values(canonical)
  ordered.forEach((f, i) => {
    if (map.has(f)) return
    // Farthest-point assignment: the dominant term is the distance to EVERY
    // colour already assigned, which spreads 71 of them as far apart as the
    // palette allows. The second term is the distance to this family's
    // neighbours in the chronological walk -- the one before, and the one after
    // when it is canonical -- which breaks ties in favour of lanes that will
    // sit next to each other. Weighted the other way round, the walk produced
    // good lane contrast and a legend full of near-duplicates.
    const near = [map.get(ordered[i - 1]), canonical[ordered[i + 1]]].filter(Boolean)
    const score = c => d3.min(taken, t => dE(c, t))
                       + 0.35 * (near.length ? d3.min(near, n => dE(c, n)) : 0)
    const pick = d3.greatest(grid, score)
    map.set(f, pick)
    taken.push(pick)
  })
  return f => map.get(f) ?? "#9c755f"     // fallback also covers the no-family group
}
top_authors_t = transpose(top_authors)
geo_t = transpose(geo)
institutions_t = transpose(institutions)
pub_authorship_t = transpose(pub_authorship)
coauth_edges_t = transpose(coauth_edges).map(r => ({ ...r, n_authors: +r.n_authors, papers: +r.papers }))

// Newman (2001) fractional collaboration strength. Each pair on an n-author
// paper earns 1/(n-1), so a 2-author paper contributes a full 1.0 to its single
// pair while a 53-author consortium contributes ~0.019 to each of its 1378
// pairs. `max_authors` lets the reader drop mega-author papers entirely.
coauth_strength = (max_authors = Infinity) => {
  // Author names contain spaces, so the composite key needs a delimiter that
  // cannot occur inside a name (same '<<|>>' convention as the bipartite chart).
  const SEP = "<<|>>"
  const w = new Map()   // "source<<|>>target" -> summed fractional weight
  for (const r of coauth_edges_t) {
    if (r.n_authors > max_authors) continue
    const k = r.source + SEP + r.target
    w.set(k, (w.get(k) ?? 0) + r.papers / (r.n_authors - 1))
  }
  return Array.from(w, ([k, weight]) => {
    const [source, target] = k.split(SEP)
    return { source, target, weight }
  })
}

// All prolific authors, regardless of the network's reactive filters — used by
// the bipartite author↔model chart so its node set stays stable.
coauth_all_authors = new Set(coauth_edges_t.flatMap(e => [e.source, e.target]))
author_affs_t = transpose(author_affs)
algorithms_t = transpose(algorithms).map(r => ({
  ...r,
  first_pub: r.first_pub ? new Date(r.first_pub) : null,
  is_dl: r.is_dl == null ? null : !!r.is_dl   // SQLite INTEGER 0/1 → JS boolean
}))

// Version-aware view of algorithms: any algorithm whose joined publications
// carry a `version` tag (currently Casanovo v1 / v2 / v5) is expanded into one
// row per version, each with its own first_pub date and a label like
// "Casanovo v2". Drives the architectures timeline so successive releases of
// the same method appear as distinct dots instead of collapsing onto the
// earliest one. All other downstream cells (counters, bipartite network,
// browse table) keep using `algorithms_t` and remain one-row-per-algorithm.
algorithms_versioned_t = {
  const pubs_for = new Map()
  for (const p of pubs_t) {
    for (const m of (p.models ?? "").split(",").map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)) {
      if (!pubs_for.has(m)) pubs_for.set(m, [])
      pubs_for.get(m).push(p)
    }
  }
  const out = []
  for (const r of algorithms_t) {
    const its_pubs = pubs_for.get(r.model) ?? []
    const versions = Array.from(new Set(its_pubs.map(p => p.version).filter(Boolean))).sort()
    if (versions.length === 0) { out.push({ ...r, base_model: r.model }); continue }
    for (const v of versions) {
      const dates = its_pubs.filter(p => p.version === v).map(p => p.date).filter(Boolean)
      const earliest = dates.length ? new Date(Math.min(...dates.map(d => +d))) : r.first_pub
      out.push({ ...r, model: `${r.model} ${v}`, version: v, base_model: r.model, first_pub: earliest })
    }
    const unversioned = its_pubs.filter(p => !p.version)
    if (unversioned.length) {
      const dates = unversioned.map(p => p.date).filter(Boolean)
      const earliest = dates.length ? new Date(Math.min(...dates.map(d => +d))) : r.first_pub
      out.push({ ...r, base_model: r.model, first_pub: earliest })
    }
  }
  return out
}
venues_t = transpose(venues)
author_details_t = transpose(author_details)

// --- links into the generated entity pages ------------------------------
// entity_slugs comes from slugs.py, the same module build_pages.py uses, so a
// link here and the page it targets can never disagree.
entity_slugs_t = transpose(entity_slugs)

slug_map = {
  const m = new Map()
  for (const r of entity_slugs_t) {
    if (!m.has(r.type)) m.set(r.type, new Map())
    m.get(r.type).set(String(r.key), r.slug)
  }
  return m
}

// page_href("authors", "Lukas Käll") -> "pages/authors/lukas-kall.html", or
// null when there is no such page. Callers MUST handle null: an author who is
// filtered out, or a venue string with no page, should render as plain text
// rather than a broken link.
page_href = (type, key) => {
  if (key == null) return null
  const slug = slug_map.get(type)?.get(String(key))
  return slug ? `pages/${type}/${slug}.html` : null
}

// Markup helper for Inputs.table cell formatters.
page_link = (type, key, label) => {
  const href = page_href(type, key)
  const text = label ?? key
  return href ? htl.html`<a href=${href}>${text}</a>` : text
}

// Wrap already-rendered d3 nodes in an SVG <a>, the way Plot does internally.
// The selection keeps referencing the ORIGINAL elements, so force-simulation
// tick handlers that set `transform` on them keep working.
//
// Both force graphs use d3.drag(), and a drag that ends on an anchor would
// otherwise navigate. So record the pointer position and swallow the click if
// it moved more than a few pixels.
// A repo can back two algorithms, so `model` reads "A / B"; link the first.
algo_href = m => page_href("algorithms", String(m ?? "").split(" / ")[0].trim())

// Where a family label should go. 26 of 52 families have a page of their own;
// the other 26 hold exactly one method, so their page would have carried that
// method's papers, authors and dates and nothing else. Rather than leave a
// lane label dead, a singleton family links straight to its one method: every
// label in the swim lane and every row of the long-view table is clickable, and
// which of the two kinds of target it has is not something a reader needs to
// know.
family_sole_method = new Map(
  d3.rollups(algorithms_t.filter(a => a.family), v => v, a => a.family)
    .filter(([, v]) => v.length === 1)
    .map(([f, v]) => [f, v[0].model])
)

family_href = f => page_href("families", f)
  ?? algo_href(family_sole_method.get(f))

svg_link_wrap = (selection, href_of) => {
  selection.each(function (d) {
    const href = href_of(d)
    if (!href) return
    const node = this
    const parent = node.parentNode
    const a = document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "a")
    a.setAttributeNS("http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink", "xlink:href", href)
    a.setAttribute("href", href)
    a.style.cursor = "pointer"
    parent.insertBefore(a, node)
    a.appendChild(node)
    let start = null
    a.addEventListener("pointerdown", ev => { start = [ev.clientX, ev.clientY] })
    a.addEventListener("click", ev => {
      if (!start) return
      const moved = Math.hypot(ev.clientX - start[0], ev.clientY - start[1])
      if (moved > 4) ev.preventDefault()   // it was a drag, not a click
    })
  })
  return selection
}

// Linkify the tick labels of a Plot ordinal axis. Matched by TEXT, never by
// index, so there is no ordering assumption to get wrong: a label that does not
// resolve simply stays plain text.
linkify_tick_labels = (chart, href_by_label) => {
  const groups = chart.querySelectorAll('g[aria-label$="axis tick label"]')
  for (const g of groups) {
    for (const text of g.querySelectorAll("text")) {
      const href = href_by_label.get(text.textContent)
      if (!href) continue
      const a = document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "a")
      a.setAttributeNS("http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink", "xlink:href", href)
      a.setAttribute("href", href)
      a.style.cursor = "pointer"
      text.parentNode.insertBefore(a, text)
      a.appendChild(text)
    }
  }
  return chart
}

// Several tables show a comma-joined list of names in one cell (authors,
// models). Link each name separately, leaving unmatched names as plain text.
page_links = (type, joined, { sep = ", ", max = Infinity } = {}) => {
  const names = String(joined ?? "").split(sep).map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)
  const shown = names.slice(0, max)
  const parts = []
  shown.forEach((n, i) => {
    if (i) parts.push(sep)
    parts.push(page_link(type, n, n))
  })
  if (names.length > shown.length) parts.push(` +${names.length - shown.length}`)
  return htl.html`${parts}`
}

// preprint_id -> published_id, from the explicit publication_version table.
pub_versions_t = transpose(pub_versions).map(r => ({
  ...r, preprint_id: +r.preprint_id, published_id: +r.published_id
}))
published_of = new Map(pub_versions_t.map(r => [r.preprint_id, r.published_id]))
preprint_of  = new Map(pub_versions_t.map(r => [r.published_id, r.preprint_id]))
citations_t      = transpose(citations)
journal_impact_t = transpose(journal_impact)
// Lookup table: journal name → 2yr citedness, for fast joins in OJS cells.
journal_impact_by_name = new Map(journal_impact_t.map(j => [j.journal, j]))
publication_impact_t = transpose(publication_impact)
publication_impact_by_pub = new Map(publication_impact_t.map(r => [r.publication_id, r]))
repo_metrics_t = transpose(repo_metrics).map(r => ({
  ...r,
  last_pushed: r.last_pushed ? new Date(r.last_pushed) : null,
  fetched_at:  r.fetched_at  ? new Date(r.fetched_at)  : null,
}))

// Some repositories back multiple catalogued algorithms (e.g. InstaNovo +
// InstaNovo-P share instadeepai/instanovo). For the two Code-activity plots
// we want ONE dot per repo — otherwise the shared bar/point appears twice
// on top of itself and the label collides. Fold rows by URL, joining the
// per-repo model names with ' / ' so the tooltip still shows which
// algorithms live in that repo. The Browse-all table below keeps the
// un-deduplicated repo_metrics_t so per-algorithm columns (family, kind)
// stay intact.
repo_metrics_by_url = {
  const grouped = new Map()
  for (const r of repo_metrics_t) {
    if (!r.url) continue
    if (!grouped.has(r.url)) grouped.set(r.url, {...r, models: [r.model]})
    else grouped.get(r.url).models.push(r.model)
  }
  return Array.from(grouped.values()).map(r => ({
    ...r,
    // 'model' overrides the single-value field with a joined label used by
    // Plot.text and the tooltip title. 'family' picks the first algorithm's
    // family for the dot color (families are usually the same when they
    // share a repo; where they differ, the first one seen wins).
    model: r.models.join(" / "),
  }))
}

// Derived counters. Everything flows from the data, no hardcoded numbers.
n_papers = pubs_t.length
n_models = algorithms_t.length
n_authors = new Set(pubs_t.flatMap(p => (p.authors ?? "").split(", ").filter(Boolean))).size
n_countries = geo_t.length
// Datasets replaced countries in the hero. n_countries stays defined because
// the geography section's own prose still reads it.
n_datasets = all_dataset_rows.length
years_with_pubs = pubs_t.map(p => p.year).filter(y => Number.isFinite(y))
first_year = Math.min(...years_with_pubs)
last_year  = Math.max(...years_with_pubs)
// First year a paper using deep learning appears in the catalog. Anchors the
// "wave" prose so the DL inflection point reads from data, not a constant.
dl_algo_names = new Set(algorithms_t.filter(a => a.is_dl === true).map(a => a.model))
first_dl_year = Math.min(...pubs_t
  .filter(p => Number.isFinite(p.year) && (p.models ?? "").split(",").map(s => s.trim()).some(m => dl_algo_names.has(m)))
  .map(p => p.year)
)
n_preprints = pubs_t.filter(p => p.type === "preprint").length
n_peer_reviewed = pubs_t.filter(p => p.type === "peer-reviewed").length
families = Array.from(new Set(algorithms_t.map(a => a.family).filter(Boolean)))

// Classification breakdowns (kind / DL / acquisition).
n_dl     = algorithms_t.filter(a => a.is_dl === true).length
n_non_dl = algorithms_t.filter(a => a.is_dl === false).length
kinds_present     = Array.from(new Set(algorithms_t.map(a => a.kind).filter(Boolean))).sort()
acq_modes_present = Array.from(new Set(algorithms_t.map(a => a.acquisition).filter(Boolean))).sort()
kind_counts = kinds_present.map(k => ({ kind: k, n: algorithms_t.filter(a => a.kind === k).length }))
acq_counts  = acq_modes_present.map(m => ({ acquisition: m, n: algorithms_t.filter(a => a.acquisition === m).length }))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
```
```{ojs}
// Lets the breakdown rows below drive the three global filters.
//
// It references the viewof ELEMENTS, not their values. In OJS that is a
// dependency on the element (stable for the life of the page) rather than on
// the value, so this cell does not re-run every time a filter changes, and
// there is no reactive loop back into the breakdown that reads it.
breakdown_apply = {
  const set = (view, value) => {
    view.value = value
    view.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", { bubbles: true }))
    // The filter panel is collapsed by default on narrow screens, where a
    // filter set from here would change page-wide state invisibly. Open it so
    // the change is legible and reversible.
    const wrap = document.querySelector(".sticky-filters")
    if (wrap) wrap.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "true")
  }
  return {
    kind:     k => set(viewof kind_filter, [k]),
    approach: v => set(viewof dl_filter, v),
    acq:      m => set(viewof acq_filter, [m])
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const kind_label = {
    "algorithm": "Algorithms",
    "post-processor": "Post-processors",
    "downstream-application": "Downstream apps",
    "adjacent": "Adjacent",
    "review": "Reviews / surveys",
    "benchmark": "Benchmarks",
    "meta": "Meta"
  }
  // Every row sets the matching global filter and lands on the papers table.
  // href does the navigation so keyboard and middle-click still work; a click
  // listener sets the filter. Only the clicked dimension is touched, so an
  // approach or acquisition choice already made is preserved.
  //
  // Handlers are attached with addEventListener AFTER building the markup,
  // not as onclick=${fn} inside the template. Quarto's OJS `html` is the
  // observablehq/stdlib one, which builds through innerHTML and cannot take a
  // function: it stringifies it, leaving a literal onclick attribute that
  // throws "Failed to read the 'onclick' property ... Unexpected token ')'".
  // Only the data-* strings survive the template, so the wiring reads them.
  //
  // Note the counts are of METHODS while the destination lists PAPERS, so the
  // number on the row is not the number of rows you land on. They answer
  // different questions; the filter is what they share.
  const row = (n, label, colour, dim, val, hint) => html`<a
      class="breakdown-row breakdown-row-link"
      href="#every-paper"
      title="${hint}"
      data-dim="${dim}" data-val="${val}">
    <span class="bk-num">${n}</span>
    <span class="bk-bar"><span class="bk-fill" style="width:${100 * n / n_models}%; background:${colour}"></span></span>
    <span class="bk-lbl">${label}</span>
  </a>`

  const root = html`<div class="breakdown-grid">
    <div class="breakdown-cell">
      <div class="breakdown-title">By kind</div>
      ${kind_counts.map(k => row(k.n, kind_label[k.kind] ?? k.kind, "#1f6feb", "kind", k.kind,
          `Filter the page to ${kind_label[k.kind] ?? k.kind} and jump to the papers table`))}
    </div>
    <div class="breakdown-cell">
      <div class="breakdown-title">By approach</div>
      ${row(n_dl, "Deep learning", "#1f6feb", "approach", "DL only",
          "Filter the page to deep-learning methods and jump to the papers table")}
      ${row(n_non_dl, "Classical", "#6f42c1", "approach", "Classical only",
          "Filter the page to classical methods and jump to the papers table")}
    </div>
    <div class="breakdown-cell">
      <div class="breakdown-title">By acquisition</div>
      ${acq_counts.map(m => row(m.n, m.acquisition, "#1a7f37", "acq", m.acquisition,
          `Filter the page to ${m.acquisition} and jump to the papers table`))}
    </div>
  </div>`

  for (const a of root.querySelectorAll("a.breakdown-row-link")) {
    a.addEventListener("click", () => {
      const { dim, val } = a.dataset
      if (dim === "kind") breakdown_apply.kind(val)
      else if (dim === "approach") breakdown_apply.approach(val)
      else if (dim === "acq") breakdown_apply.acq(val)
    })
  }
  return root
}
```

::: {.scope-banner}
**Scope.** A comprehensive map of *de novo* peptide sequencing covering core **algorithms**, **post-processors** (re-rankers / FDR / refinement), **downstream applications** (immunopeptidomics, metaproteomics, cyclopeptides), **adjacent** tools (database-search hybrids, glycopeptide pipelines), **reviews / surveys**, and **benchmarks**. Both **deep-learning** and **classical** methods are tracked; the filters below let you slice by approach, acquisition mode (DDA / DIA), and paper kind. Want a paper added? See [Contributing](#contributing).
:::

```{=html}
<script>
// Tap-to-toggle the sticky filter pane. Always wires the click handler on
// every viewport. The @media (max-width:768px) CSS rule is what actually
// hides/shows the body based on aria-expanded, so on desktop a tap just
// rotates the (display:none) chevron with no visible effect.
(() => {
  const wireUp = () => {
    const wrap = document.querySelector('.sticky-filters');
    if (!wrap) return;
    const header = wrap.querySelector('.sticky-filters-header');
    if (!header) return;
    const toggle = () => {
      const open = wrap.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
      wrap.setAttribute('aria-expanded', open ? 'false' : 'true');
      header.setAttribute('aria-expanded', open ? 'false' : 'true');
    };
    header.addEventListener('click', toggle);
    header.addEventListener('keydown', e => {
      if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); toggle(); }
    });
  };
  if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', wireUp);
  } else {
    wireUp();
  }
})();
</script>
```

## The architectures

*De novo* sequencing has cycled through several methodological families: first hand-engineered dynamic programming and learning-to-rank, then a long stretch of CNN+RNN models, then transformers, GNNs, NAR variants, and most recently diffusion. Use the filters to focus on one slice of the field; hover a dot to read the method's signature contribution, or click a family name on the left for every method in it.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof family_filter = Inputs.checkbox(families, { label: "Families", value: families })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
innovations_timeline = {
  // Colour comes from the SHARED family scale, which every family-coloured chart
  // on the page uses, so a family is the same colour in the swim lane, the
  // code-activity scatter and the bipartite graph. It used to stop at these 13:
  // the other 36 shared one neutral grey, so most of the chart read as a single
  // undifferentiated family. See family_color_scale for how the rest are
  // generated. Defining a second local generator here would be the bug that
  // scale exists to prevent.
  const color_of = f => family_color_scale(f)

  const family_first = d3.rollup(
    algorithms_versioned_t.filter(a => a.family && a.first_pub),
    v => d3.min(v, a => a.first_pub),
    a => a.family
  )
  // Lanes stack UPWARD from y = 0, so the array runs latest-first to put the
  // earliest family at the top, matching "The long view". Family name breaks a
  // tie so the order is deterministic; an undated family sorts as latest.
  const LATEST = new Date(8640000000000)
  const lane_sort = (a, b) =>
    d3.descending(family_first.get(a) ?? LATEST, family_first.get(b) ?? LATEST)
    || d3.descending(a, b)
  const all_families = Array.from(new Set(
    algorithms_versioned_t.filter(a => a.family).map(a => a.family))).sort(lane_sort)

  // Lane geometry is measured in PIXELS, because the thing that must not
  // collide is a rendered label. It used to be assigned from a date gap against
  // a per-family tier list sized to the BUSIEST family, which handed a 2-unit
  // band 38 tier positions ~4 px apart and piled its labels on top of each
  // other: 7 label-label and 15 label-dot collisions, measured in the DOM.
  // Packing by measured label width removes the class rather than retuning it,
  // and it makes the hand-tuned band_heights table unnecessary -- a lane is now
  // exactly as tall as the rows its labels need.
  const ROW_PX = 43           // 24 px for up to two label lines, 3 gap, 16 dot
  const DOT_IN_ROW_PX = 35    // dot centre from the row top, label in the 24 above
  const CHAR_PX = 5.7         // mean advance of 10 px bold Source Sans Pro
  const LABEL_GAP_PX = 8      // clear air between two labels sharing a row
  const PLOT_WIDTH_PX = 1130  // width 1400 minus marginLeft 210 and marginRight 60

  // Apply every filter (family, kind, approach, acquisition) up front.
  const matches_filters = a => {
    if (!a.first_pub || !a.family) return false
    if (!family_filter.includes(a.family)) return false
    if (!kind_filter.includes(a.kind)) return false
    if (dl_filter === "DL only"        && a.is_dl !== true)  return false
    if (dl_filter === "Classical only" && a.is_dl !== false) return false
    if (a.acquisition && !acq_filter.includes(a.acquisition)) return false
    return true
  }

  // Only include bands that have at least one surviving model. Every present
  // family gets a lane: the lane list used to be intersected with the thirteen
  // hand-tuned ones, which dropped the other 36 entirely and made checking any
  // one of them produce an empty chart.
  const surviving = algorithms_versioned_t.filter(matches_filters)
  const present = new Set(surviving.map(a => a.family))
  const visible_bands = Array.from(present).sort(lane_sort)

  // Wrap the display label onto two lines at a word boundary when it exceeds
  // the max width (Plot renders \n as separate tspans). Same helper as the
  // application-areas chart below -- labels here can be long too
  // ('MALDI-QIT de novo sequencing', 'Robust FL-Sequencing', etc).
  const wrap_label = (s, max_chars = 22) => {
    if (!s || s.length <= max_chars) return s
    const words = s.split(' ')
    if (words.length === 1) return s
    let line1 = ''
    let i = 0
    while (i < words.length && (line1 ? line1.length + 1 + words[i].length : words[i].length) <= max_chars) {
      line1 = line1 ? `${line1} ${words[i]}` : words[i]
      i++
    }
    if (!line1) { line1 = words[0]; i = 1 }
    const line2 = words.slice(i).join(' ')
    return line2 ? `${line1}\n${line2}` : line1
  }
  // Half the width a label will occupy, floored at the dot so a one-word label
  // still reserves the dot's own footprint.
  const half_px = label => Math.max(9,
    d3.max(String(label).split('\n'), l => l.length) * CHAR_PX / 2)

  const rows = surviving
    .filter(a => present.has(a.family))
    .map(a => ({ ...a, label: wrap_label(a.model) }))
    .sort((a, b) => a.first_pub - b.first_pub)

  // The x domain is padded by exactly the widest label's half width, solved for
  // rather than guessed: with plot width W, data span S days and pad P days,
  // P * W / (S + 2P) = half, so P = half * S / (W - 2 * half). An eight-month
  // guess left 'PepSeq' 7 px outside the frame.
  const x_min = d3.min(rows, a => a.first_pub) ?? new Date(Date.UTC(1984, 0, 1))
  const x_max = d3.max(rows, a => a.first_pub) ?? new Date()
  const max_half = d3.max(rows, a => half_px(a.label)) ?? 9
  const span_days = Math.max(365, (x_max - x_min) / 86400000)
  const pad_days = Math.min(3650,
    max_half * span_days / Math.max(1, PLOT_WIDTH_PX - 2 * max_half))
  const x_pad_min = new Date(+x_min - pad_days * 86400000)
  const x_pad_max = new Date(+x_max + pad_days * 86400000)
  const px_per_day = PLOT_WIDTH_PX / ((x_pad_max - x_pad_min) / 86400000)
  const x_px = d => (d - x_pad_min) / 86400000 * px_per_day

  // Greedy first-fit row packing per family: a row is reused only when the two
  // labels cannot touch. Rows are filled in date order, so an early paper never
  // gets pushed down by a later one.
  const row_right = new Map()   // `${family}|${row}` -> right edge in px
  const rows_used = new Map()   // family -> how many rows it needed
  const placed = []
  for (const row of rows) {
    const cx = x_px(row.first_pub)
    const half = half_px(row.label)
    let r = 0
    for (;; r++) {
      const key = `${row.family}|${r}`
      const right = row_right.get(key)
      if (right === undefined || cx - half >= right + LABEL_GAP_PX) {
        row_right.set(key, cx + half)
        break
      }
    }
    rows_used.set(row.family, Math.max(rows_used.get(row.family) ?? 0, r + 1))
    placed.push({ ...row, row: r })
  }

  // Stack bands bottom-to-top, each exactly as tall as its packed rows.
  // visible_bands is already latest-first and y grows upward, so walking it in
  // order puts the latest family at the bottom and the earliest at the top,
  // which is the order "The long view" uses. Reversing here would insist on
  // the opposite and did: the first cut of this put Sparse autoencoder on top.
  let y_cursor = 0
  const bands = visible_bands.map(family => {
    const h = Math.max(1, rows_used.get(family) ?? 1) * ROW_PX
    const band = { family, y0: y_cursor, y1: y_cursor + h, center: y_cursor + h / 2, height: h }
    y_cursor += h
    return band
  })
  const total_height = y_cursor
  const band_index = new Map(bands.map(b => [b.family, b]))

  // Row 0 is the TOP row of its band (y grows upward here), so within a lane the
  // rows also read earliest-first.
  const items = placed.map(d => {
    const band = band_index.get(d.family)
    return { ...d, y: band.y1 - d.row * ROW_PX - DOT_IN_ROW_PX }
  })

  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: 1400,
    // total_height is in pixels, so 1 y unit = 1 px: the row packing above
    // computed real label geometry and the plot must not rescale it.
    height: Math.max(240, total_height + 60),
    marginLeft: 210,   // measured 49 px, then 10 px still over at 195
    marginRight: 60,
    marginTop: 20,
    marginBottom: 40,
    x: { type: "time", label: "First publication →", domain: [x_pad_min, x_pad_max], grid: true },
    y: { domain: [0, total_height], axis: null },
    color: {
      domain: all_families,
      range: all_families.map(color_of),
      legend: false
    },
    marks: [
      // Background band per family, extended to the padded x domain so edge labels stay inside.
      Plot.rect(bands, {
        x1: () => x_pad_min, x2: () => x_pad_max,
        y1: "y0", y2: "y1",
        fill: "family",
        fillOpacity: 0.09
      }),
      // Thin separators between bands
      Plot.ruleY(bands.flatMap(b => [b.y0, b.y1]), { stroke: "#ddd", strokeWidth: 0.5 }),
      // Left-edge family label, and a link: a family with two or more methods
      // has a page collecting them, and a one-method family sends the reader
      // to its single method instead. See family_href.
      Plot.text(bands, {
        x: () => x_pad_min,
        y: "center",
        text: "family",
        textAnchor: "end",
        dx: -8,
        fontSize: 12,
        fontWeight: "bold",
        fill: "family",
        href: d => family_href(d.family),
        target: "_self"
      }),
      // Rich HTML tooltips are wired below via a scoped
      // chart.querySelectorAll('g[aria-label="dot"] circle') selector on the
      // rendered SVG; no Plot tip is used here.
      Plot.dot(items, {
        x: "first_pub",
        y: "y",
        fill: "family",
        r: 7,
        stroke: "white",
        strokeWidth: 1.5,
        // Plot wraps each mark in an SVG <a> itself, which sidesteps the
        // descending-radius re-sort that makes DOM-index binding fragile here.
        href: d => algo_href(d.base_model ?? d.model),
        target: "_self"
      }),
      // One label per dot, always directly above it. The old above-or-below
      // split was there to buy vertical space from a fixed band height; the row
      // packing gives every label its own 24 px instead, so a single anchor is
      // both simpler and collision-free. Names over ~22 chars wrap onto two
      // lines; the full name stays in the tooltip.
      Plot.text(items, {
        x: "first_pub",
        y: "y",
        text: "label",
        textAnchor: "middle",
        lineAnchor: "bottom",
        dy: -11,
        fontSize: 10,
        fontWeight: "bold",
        fill: "family"
      })
    ]
  })

  // Rich .map-tooltip on the Plot.dot circles — matches the HTML tooltip style
  // used across the world-map / co-auth / bipartite / Sankey / citation-arc
  // charts. Plot renders dots in the order of the input `items` array, so we
  // bind by DOM order.
  const arch_tooltip = html`<div class="map-tooltip" role="tooltip" aria-hidden="true"></div>`
  const move_arch_tip = ev => {
    const pad = 12
    const box = arch_tooltip.getBoundingClientRect()
    const left = Math.min(ev.clientX + pad, window.innerWidth  - box.width  - pad)
    const top  = Math.min(ev.clientY + pad, window.innerHeight - box.height - pad)
    arch_tooltip.style.left = `${Math.max(pad, left)}px`
    arch_tooltip.style.top  = `${Math.max(pad, top)}px`
  }
  // Plot silently ignores the `className: 'arch-dot'` mark option we passed —
  // it labels dot marks with aria-label='dot' instead. querySelectorAll is
  // scoped to *this* chart's DOM so we won't pick up other Plot.dot charts.
  const arch_dot_circles = chart.querySelectorAll('g[aria-label="dot"] circle')
  arch_dot_circles.forEach((circle, i) => {
    const d = items[i]
    if (!d) return
    circle.style.cursor = "pointer"
    circle.setAttribute("aria-label", `${d.model}. ${d.family}. First publication ${d.first_pub.toISOString().slice(0,10)}.`)
    circle.addEventListener("mouseenter", ev => {
      arch_tooltip.replaceChildren(html`<div>
        <div class="map-tooltip-title">${d.model}</div>
        <div class="map-tooltip-meta">${d.first_pub.toISOString().slice(0,10)}</div>
        <div class="map-tooltip-row">
          <span class="map-tooltip-swatch" style=${`background:${color_of(d.family)}`}></span>
          <span>${d.family}</span>
        </div>
        ${d.description ? html`<div class="map-tooltip-meta" style="margin-top:6px; max-width:280px; white-space:normal;">${d.description}</div>` : ""}
      </div>`)
      arch_tooltip.classList.add("visible")
      arch_tooltip.setAttribute("aria-hidden", "false")
      move_arch_tip(ev)
    })
    circle.addEventListener("mousemove", move_arch_tip)
    circle.addEventListener("mouseleave", () => {
      arch_tooltip.classList.remove("visible")
      arch_tooltip.setAttribute("aria-hidden", "true")
    })
  })

  // Wrap in a horizontally-scrollable container with a fullscreen button.
  return html`<div class="chart-wrap">
    <button class="fs-btn" onclick="
      const el = this.parentElement;
      if (document.fullscreenElement) document.exitFullscreen();
      else el.requestFullscreen();
    ">⛶ Fullscreen</button>
    <div class="chart-scroll">${chart}</div>
    ${arch_tooltip}
  </div>`
}
```

## The long view

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Every methodological family in the catalog, placed at the moment it first
appeared. The span runs from **${ff_first_year}** to **${ff_last_year}**,
**${ff_span}** years, across **${ff_rows.length}** distinct families. This is the
only view that fits them on one screen: the chart above gives each family a lane
too, but spends 20 of its 91 height units on Transformer (AR) alone, and the
volume chart below counts papers per year, where the early era is a one-paper
sliver against a linear axis. Families appear here in the same order as the
lanes above.`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ff_rows = transpose(family_firsts)
  .map(r => ({ ...r, date: new Date(r.first_date), year: +r.first_date.slice(0, 4) }))
  .sort((a, b) => a.date - b.date)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ff_first_year = d3.min(ff_rows, r => r.year)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ff_last_year = d3.max(ff_rows, r => r.year)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ff_span = ff_last_year - ff_first_year
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Approach is derived from the introducing method's is_deep_learning, not from
// the family name: several families (Graph / DP + neural network, Sparse
// autoencoder) are only classifiable that way, and NULL is its own case rather
// than being folded into classical.
// A label flips to the left of its dot once the dot is far enough right that a
// ~40-character name would leave the plot area. 0.62 of the span was chosen
// from the measurement: it flips every family that overflowed and none that
// did not.
ff_label_flips = d => {
  const lo = new Date(`${ff_first_year - 1}-01-01`).getTime()
  const hi = new Date(`${ff_last_year + 1}-01-01`).getTime()
  return (d.date.getTime() - lo) / (hi - lo) > 0.62
}

ff_approach = r => r.first_is_dl === true || r.first_is_dl === 1 ? "Deep learning"
              : r.first_is_dl === false || r.first_is_dl === 0 ? "Classical"
              : "Not applicable"
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 1100,
  height: 22 * ff_rows.length + 70,
  marginLeft: 250,
  marginRight: 100,  // flipping late labels left cut 182 px of overflow to
                     // 68; this clears the rest without crushing the axis
  marginTop: 34,
  x: {
    label: "First appearance",
    grid: true,
    // Fixed to whole years so the 1984-to-1994 gap reads as a real decade of
    // quiet rather than being compressed away by a data-driven domain.
    domain: [new Date(`${ff_first_year - 1}-01-01`), new Date(`${ff_last_year + 1}-01-01`)]
  },
  y: { label: null, domain: ff_rows.map(r => r.family), tickSize: 0 },
  color: {
    legend: true,
    domain: ["Classical", "Deep learning", "Not applicable"],
    range: ["#6c757d", "#C44E52", "#b0b7bd"]
  },
  marks: [
    // A rule from the axis to the dot: without it, a 49-row dot plot is hard to
    // read across 250px of label gutter.
    Plot.ruleY(ff_rows, {
      y: "family",
      x1: new Date(`${ff_first_year - 1}-01-01`),
      x2: "date",
      stroke: "#e3e6e9",
      strokeWidth: 1
    }),
    Plot.dot(ff_rows, {
      x: "date",
      y: "family",
      r: r => 3 + Math.min(r.n_methods, 9) * 0.55,
      fill: ff_approach,
      stroke: "white",
      strokeWidth: 0.8,
      tip: true,
      channels: {
        "introduced by": "first_method",
        "paper": "first_title",
        "venue": "first_journal",
        "methods in this family": "n_methods"
      }
    }),
    // Labels sit to the RIGHT of the dot, except for late families, whose
    // labels would run off the chart: measured 182 px of overflow, worst case
    // "Sparse autoencoder interpretability of InstaNovo" at 2026-06-25.
    // Flipping them to the left of the dot costs nothing, because the right
    // side of a late dot is empty by definition, whereas reserving 215 px of
    // marginRight would squeeze 42 years of timeline into less width.
    //
    // TWO MARKS, not one with functions. Plot's `dx`, `dy` and `textAnchor` are
    // CONSTANT options, not channels: passing a function silently applies
    // neither, so the first attempt at this left every label centred on its own
    // dot with dx 0. That is what put a dot in the middle of all 49 names, and
    // it was invisible in the code because a function is a perfectly legal
    // value. Measured before: 49 label-over-dot collisions, 9 px each.
    //
    // dx of 11 clears the largest dot, whose radius is 3 + 9 * 0.55 = 7.95.
    Plot.text(ff_rows.filter(d => !ff_label_flips(d)), {
      x: "date",
      y: "family",
      text: "first_method",
      dx: 11,
      textAnchor: "start",
      fontSize: 10,
      fill: "#444"
    }),
    Plot.text(ff_rows.filter(ff_label_flips), {
      x: "date",
      y: "family",
      text: "first_method",
      dx: -11,
      textAnchor: "end",
      fontSize: 10,
      fill: "#444"
    })
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(
  ff_rows.map(r => ({
    "First seen": r.first_date,
    "Family": r.family,
    "Approach": ff_approach(r),
    "Introduced by": r.first_method,
    "Methods since": r.n_methods,
    "Paper": r.first_title,
    "Venue": r.first_journal || ""
  })),
  {
    rows: 20,
    sort: "First seen",
    reverse: false,
    layout: "auto",
    // Same cell-linking convention as the other tables: an internal detail page,
    // plus an arrow to the publisher where there is one. Inputs.table passes the
    // index into the ORIGINAL array, not the sorted position, so ff_rows[i] is the
    // right row however the reader sorts the table.
    format: {
      // The family name links to the family's own page where it has one, and to
      // its single method where it does not; same rule as the swim-lane labels.
      "Family": f => {
        const href = family_href(f)
        return href ? htl.html`<a href=${href}>${f}</a>` : f
      },
      "Introduced by": (m, i) => page_link("algorithms", ff_rows[i].first_method, m),
      "Paper": (t, i) => {
        const row = ff_rows[i]
        const internal = page_href("publications", row.first_pub_id)
        const external = row.first_url || (row.first_doi ? `https://doi.org/${row.first_doi}` : null)
        const label = internal ? htl.html`<a href=${internal}>${t}</a>` : t
        return external
          ? htl.html`${label} <a href="${external}" target="_blank" rel="noopener"
              title="Publisher / DOI" style="text-decoration:none">↗</a>`
          : label
      },
      "Venue": v => v ? page_link("venues", v, v) : ""
    },
    width: { "First seen": 92, "Methods since": 92, "Approach": 100 }
  }
)
```

## How they score

Everything above is what the methods ARE. This is how they do, on the field's two
public benchmarks. Neither is a leaderboard someone can game by reporting their
own numbers: both run the tools themselves and publish the results as data.

[**denovo_benchmarks**](https://github.com/bittremieuxlab/denovo_benchmarks) runs
every tool in its own container over 84 datasets, against the same ground-truth
PSMs and the same metric code, and asks how a method holds up across
instruments, organisms, digests and modifications. That is the first four charts
here.

[**ProteoBench**](https://proteobench.cubimed.rub.de/denovo_DDA_HCD) takes one
dataset, the published nine-species benchmark, and accepts submitted runs with
their parameters recorded. That is the last two. It answers a different
question: with these settings, on this data, where does the tool land.
